# What LightHit computes {#sec-overview}

## The physical question {#sec-overview-question}

A charged particle crosses a volume of water and emits Cherenkov light along
its path. Some of that light reaches an optical module; most of it does not.
Between emission and arrival a photon may be absorbed, or may change direction
one or more times, so that it arrives later than a straight line would allow
and from a direction the source never pointed in. The module converts a
fraction of what arrives into photoelectrons, and the readout assigns them to
time bins.

The quantity this package computes is the **expected number of photoelectrons**
in module $d$ and time bin $b$,
$$
N_{db}\;=\;\bigl\langle\,\text{photoelectrons registered by module }d
\text{ in }[t_b,t_{b+1})\,\bigr\rangle ,
$$ {#eq-overview-observable}
together with the integrated charge
$$
Q_d=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\!N_d(t)\,\mathrm dt=\tilde N_d(\omega=0),
$$ {#eq-overview-charge}
where $N_d(t)$ is the rate whose integral over a bin is
@eq-overview-observable. The charge is evaluated directly at zero frequency and
is **not** the sum of the finite set of bins. The two would agree only for a
window that contains the whole signal and an exact inversion of it, and neither
holds in general: @sec-overview-example reports a configuration in which they
differ by $1.3\%$. Wherever this book quotes a charge it means
@eq-overview-charge.

The angle brackets are an ensemble average over photon histories, not one
realisation of them. A Monte Carlo code estimates the same average by sampling
histories; LightHit evaluates it by solving the transport equation that the
average obeys, once per spectral node, and then contracting the solution with
the source and with the module.

The reason for solving rather than sampling is not that sampling is
intrinsically expensive. A Monte Carlo pays per photon propagated: its cost is
set by the light yield of the event and by the statistical error that is
acceptable, not by the number of source--module pairs. What does scale with
pairs is the *deterministic* alternative to a solve --- evaluating a response
element by element and module by module. A simulated shower is delivered as
$10^5$--$10^6$ emitting steps and an array such as Baikal-GVD has some
$2\times10^3$ modules, so that route costs $10^8$--$10^9$ evaluations per
event.

Solving pays once for the medium instead, and it is worth being precise about
what "once" buys. For a point isotropic source seen by a directional module,
the answer in a homogeneous unbounded medium depends on the distance and on one
angle. For a *directed* emitting element seen by a directional module it
depends on the distance and on three independent angular invariants, since
three unit vectors are involved --- the emission axis, the module axis, and the
line joining the two --- and a rotation-invariant, parity-even medium leaves
exactly three of their mutual cosines. Either way the answer is a function of a
few variables, which is what makes it tabulable once and reusable for every
element, every event and every module orientation (@sec-cache-and-memory).

This chapter states what is computed, fixes the observable and the
assumptions, and lays out the whole calculation as a sequence of steps. Each
later chapter expands one of those steps.

## Assumptions and definitions {#sec-overview-assumptions}

**The medium.** Homogeneous, unbounded and isotropic. At wavelength $\lambda$
it is described by an absorption coefficient $\mu_a(\lambda)$, a scattering
coefficient $\mu_s(\lambda)$, a Henyey--Greenstein asymmetry $g$, a phase
refractive index $n_{\rm ph}(\lambda)$ and a group refractive index
$n_g(\lambda)$. Scattering is elastic: a photon changes direction but not
wavelength, so the wavelengths decouple and each one is solved on its own.
Polarisation, boundaries between water and anything else, and shadowing by the
detector structure are outside the model.

Two refractive indices appear because they answer two different questions. The
Cherenkov emission angle and the spectral yield are set by the phase index; the
speed at which a pulse travels between emission and arrival is
$v_g=c_0/n_g$. Using one where the other belongs is a silent error of a few
per cent in time, and @sec-spectral-rte keeps them apart by name.

**What is transported.** The spectral angular intensity
$I_\lambda(\mathbf x,\hat s,t)$ is defined so that
$$
\mathrm dN=\frac{I_\lambda}{v_g}\,
\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm d\Omega\,\mathrm d\lambda
$$ {#eq-overview-intensity}
is the expected number of photons in the spatial volume $\mathrm d^3x$ whose
direction of travel lies in $\mathrm d\Omega$ about $\hat s$ and whose
wavelength lies in $\mathrm d\lambda$ about $\lambda$. With metres,
nanoseconds and nanometres,
$[I_\lambda]=\text{photon}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm{ns}^{-1}\mathrm{sr}^{-1}
\mathrm{nm}^{-1}$. @sec-spectral-rte derives the equation $I_\lambda$ obeys.

**The module.** Module $d$ sits at $\mathbf x_d$, has geometrical area $A_d$,
a spectral efficiency $\epsilon_d(\lambda)$ that collects quantum efficiency
and the transmission of the glass and gel, and an angular acceptance that
depends only on the angle between the arrival direction and the module axis.

Two unit vectors describe that axis and they point opposite ways, so the
convention is fixed once here and used without exception. The module stores
$\hat o_d$, the direction from the module towards the hemisphere it accepts; a
module aimed at the source has $\hat o_d$ pointing at the source. A photon
arriving head-on therefore *travels* along
$$
\hat n_d=-\,\hat o_d,
$$ {#eq-overview-orientation}
and it is $\hat n_d$, not $\hat o_d$, that the acceptance is a function of:
$A(\hat s\cdot\hat n_d)$ is $A(+1)$ for a head-on photon and $A(-1)$ for one
arriving from directly behind the module. In the code $\hat o_d$ is
`DetectorArray.orientations`, $\hat n_d$ is formed from it on one line of the
transport routine, and @sec-optical-module shows that this is the only place
the sign is applied.

**The observable.** Collecting these,
$$
N_{db}=A_d\int_{t_b}^{t_{b+1}}\!\!\mathrm dt
\int\!\mathrm d\lambda\;\epsilon_d(\lambda)
\int_{S^2}\!\mathrm d\hat s\;A(\hat s\cdot\hat n_d)\,
I_\lambda(\mathbf x_d,\hat s,t).
$$ {#eq-overview-pe}
The units cancel to a pure count: $\mathrm m^2$ from $A_d$, $\mathrm{ns}$ from
$\mathrm dt$, $\mathrm{nm}$ from $\mathrm d\lambda$ and $\mathrm{sr}$ from
$\mathrm d\hat s$ exhaust the units of $I_\lambda$, and $\epsilon_d$ and $A$
are dimensionless. @eq-overview-pe is the definition of everything the package
reports; every later chapter computes one factor of it.

What is *not* in @eq-overview-pe is as important. There is no trigger, no
single-photoelectron charge distribution, no transit-time spread beyond an
optional Gaussian smearing, and no noise. The output is the expected
photoelectron content of an event: the input to a readout simulation, not its
output.

## Derivation {#sec-overview-derivation}

The transfer equation is linear in the source, and the medium is homogeneous
and unbounded. Those two facts, and nothing else, are what make the
calculation affordable; the whole scheme is their consequence.

Linearity means that the intensity produced by a source $q_\lambda$ is
$$
I_\lambda(\mathbf x,\hat s,t)=\int\!\mathrm d^3x'\,\mathrm dt'\!\int_{S^2}\!
\mathrm d\hat s'\;
G_\lambda(\mathbf x-\mathbf x',\hat s,\hat s',t-t')\,
q_\lambda(\mathbf x',\hat s',t'),
$$ {#eq-overview-superposition}
where the Green's function $G_\lambda$ depends on the *difference* of positions
and times because the medium is homogeneous and does not change. An event with
$10^5$ emitting elements is a sum of $10^5$ shifted and rotated copies of the
same $G_\lambda$, so the event never enters the solve: it enters the
contraction afterwards.

Substituting @eq-overview-superposition into @eq-overview-pe leaves two
angular integrals, one over the emission direction and one over the arrival
direction. The second can be moved onto the Green's function before the source
is known. Write the module functional as
$$
R_d[I]=\int_{S^2}\mathrm d\hat s\,A(\hat s\cdot\hat n_d)\,I(\mathbf x_d,\hat s),
$$
The adjoint formulation of @sec-fourier-adjoint expands $A$ in spherical
harmonics and solves the small set of resolvent rows required by its measured
bandwidth. Those rows depend on the medium, not on the event or the orientation
of a particular module; source and module rotations enter in the later
contraction. One medium solve can therefore serve every source position and
module orientation.

The remaining $\mathbf x$ and $t$ dependence is handled by transforming. In an
unbounded homogeneous medium the streaming operator
$v_g^{-1}\partial_t+\hat s\cdot\nabla$ becomes multiplication under
$$
\tilde f(\mathbf k,\omega)=\int f(\mathbf x,t)\,
e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x+i\omega t}\,\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm dt,
$$ {#eq-overview-transform}
and what is left at each $(\mathbf k,\omega)$ is an algebraic problem on the
sphere of directions. Expanded in spherical harmonics it is tridiagonal, and
@sec-angular-system solves it with an exact treatment of the infinite tail
above the truncation degree rather than by discarding it.

Three properties of the answer are used throughout and are worth naming here.
First, the solution splits by **scattering order** --- light that arrived
unscattered, light that scattered exactly once, and light that scattered twice
or more --- and the three parts are computed by different means because they
have different singularities, not by subtracting large numbers from each other
(@sec-scattering-orders). Second, the unscattered and once-scattered parts are
singular in physical time, so inverting them from a finite frequency grid is
numerically hostile; how much of that is avoided depends on the route. The
production route of this book --- a directed source and a module with a
direction --- folds the finite bin analytically onto the **unscattered** part
only, and inverts orders $1$ and $\ge2$ together from frequency. The
point-source route with an isotropic receiver folds orders $0$ *and* $1$,
using the closed form of the once-scattered arrival in physical time
(@sec-time-and-bins). Where this book says "analytic binning" it names which of
the two it means. Third, the transformed answer depends on the
geometry only through $r=|\mathbf r|$ and a small number of angular indices,
which is what makes a radial table --- the cache --- both possible and
worthwhile (@sec-cache-and-memory).

## The discrete algorithm {#sec-overview-algorithm}

The production route runs the following steps in order. Each is expanded in the
chapter named beside it.

1. **Choose spectral nodes.** Replace $\int\mathrm d\lambda$ in
   @eq-overview-pe by a Gauss--Legendre rule $\{\lambda_j,w_j\}$ over the band
   where the medium and the module are both defined (@sec-rte-to-pe).
2. **Sample the medium at each node.** Interpolate
   $\mu_a,\mu_s,n_{\rm ph},n_g$ to $\lambda_j$; each node becomes an
   independent monochromatic problem (@sec-spectral-rte).
3. **Solve the angular system.** For each $(\mathbf k,\omega)$ solve the
   tridiagonal $m$ blocks with the exact free tail for the harmonic rows required
   by the module-acceptance bandwidth (@sec-fourier-adjoint,
   @sec-angular-system).
4. **Separate the scattering orders** into $0$, $1$ and $\ge2$ at the level of
   the angular solution (@sec-scattering-orders).
5. **Invert in $\mathbf k$ and cache.** Contract against spherical Bessel
   functions to obtain radial multipoles on a radial grid, and store them
   (@sec-scattering-orders, @sec-cache-and-memory).
6. **Compile the source.** Turn the event into emitting elements carrying two
   spectral fields, and deposit them onto a grid in the frame of the event's
   own axis (@sec-cherenkov-source, @sec-track-and-shower).
7. **Contract source with module.** Combine the compiled source, the cached
   radial multipoles and the module acceptance through the exact azimuthal
   blocks, computing the unscattered term separately from the exact arrival
   direction of each element (@sec-directional-om).
8. **Sum over wavelength.** Weight by $w_j$, $\epsilon_d(\lambda_j)$ and $A_d$
   and sum over nodes, which is where @eq-overview-pe is finally assembled
   (@sec-rte-to-pe).
9. **Return to time.** Fold the finite bins analytically onto the unscattered
   order and invert the scattered orders from frequency; on the point-source
   route order $1$ is folded analytically as well (@sec-time-and-bins).

One step sits outside this list because it is an optimisation rather than a
stage of the physics: before step 7 is run at every frequency, the charge of
every module is evaluated at $\omega=0$ alone and modules below a threshold are
carried as charge without time bins (@sec-weak-module-threshold).

## Correspondence with the code {#sec-overview-code}

| Quantity | Where it appears | Symbol | Route |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| $\{\lambda_j,w_j\}$ | step 1 | `lighthit.model.WavelengthQuadrature.gauss_legendre` | both |
| $\mu_a(\lambda),\mu_s(\lambda),n_{\rm ph}(\lambda),n_g(\lambda)$ | step 2 | `lighthit.model.SpectralMedium.sample`, `.band` | both |
| $A_d$, $\epsilon_d(\lambda)$, $A(\cdot)$, $\hat o_d$ | @eq-overview-pe | `lighthit.model.DetectorArray` | both |
| Measured acceptance bandwidth $L_A$ | step 3 | `lighthit.directional.acceptance_bandwidth` | both |
| Acceptance multipoles $\alpha_\lambda$ | steps 3, 7 | `lighthit.cache.acceptance_coefficients` | both |
| Event as emitting elements | step 6 | `lighthit.sources.SpectralLightElements` | both |
| Angular solve, azimuthal blocks with exact free tail | step 3 | `lighthit.angular.resolvent_rows` | production |
| Radial tables of those blocks | step 5 | `lighthit.directional.DirectionalCache.build` | production |
| Unscattered term, exact per element | steps 7, 9 | `lighthit.ballistic.ballistic_directional` | production |
| Angular solve split into orders $0,1,\ge2$ | steps 3--4 | `lighthit.angular.angular_components` | $m=0$ |
| Radial multipoles $M_l(r,\omega)$ | step 5 | `lighthit.cache.ResponseCache.build` | $m=0$ |
| Once-scattered term folded in physical time | step 9 | `lighthit.single.single_bins` | $m=0$ |
| Frequency-to-bin inversion of the scattered orders | step 9 | `lighthit.readout.inverse_bins` | both |
| Steps 1--9 as one call | all | `lighthit.transport.TransportKernel.transport` | both |
| $N_{db}$, $Q_d$ and the run metadata | output | `lighthit.transport.TransportResponse` | both |

Two routes are distinguished in the last column and the distinction matters
for every chapter that follows. **Production** is the route this book follows
end to end: a directed source read by a module that looks in a definite
direction, which needs the azimuthal blocks of @sec-directional-om and their
own radial tables. **$m=0$** is the route for a point isotropic source, where
the module acceptance enters as a single multipole contraction and one
azimuthal block suffices; it is derived first because it is simpler, it remains
the route for a calibration flash, and it is the reference against which the
production route is checked. Citing one where the other is meant is therefore a
category error, not a harmless change of notation.

Numerical settings that appear in the steps above --- the truncation degrees,
the frequency and radial grids, the threshold --- are all fields of
`lighthit.transport.KernelConfig`, and their effect on the answer is the
subject of @sec-validation.

## A worked number {#sec-overview-example}

The example uses public parameters only: no measured optical table and no
stored event file is read. A synthetic spectral medium is defined over
400--550 nm with $g=0.9$, absorption between $0.021$ and $0.090\,\mathrm
m^{-1}$ and scattering between $0.013$ and $0.030\,\mathrm m^{-1}$. The source
is a straight $\beta=1$ track of length 20 m, rising along $+z$ from
$(0,0,-10)\,\mathrm m$, which the compiler turns into 80 emitting elements with
none dropped at the Cherenkov threshold. Five modules of radius
$0.2159\,\mathrm m$ and flat efficiency $0.25$ carry the quadratic acceptance
$A(x)=0.40+0.48x+0.12x^2$, which is positive on the whole interval and
therefore band-limited exactly at Legendre degree 2.

The numerical settings have production size: 41 frequencies from 0 to
$0.15\,\mathrm{rad/ns}$, 40 bins of 20 ns spanning $-60$ to $740\,\mathrm{ns}$
relative to the first possible arrival, scattering degree 24, source degree 32,
azimuthal degree 4, radial range 3--300 m on 220 nodes, nine spectral nodes,
and a threshold of $0.01$ photoelectrons. The cache's angular solve is forced to
the NumPy reference backend for this example; the event contraction still uses
the fused Numba implementation when Numba is installed. Reproduce with

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 NUMBA_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  python scripts/run_overview_example.py --output .build/overview --repeats 2
```

The listed BLAS, OpenMP and Numba thread controls are fixed to one; the exact backend
used by each stage and all relevant package versions are recorded in
`docs/overview-example/overview.json`. There is no warm-up, and two repetitions
in one process must agree exactly. The route uses no random numbers, so the
spread within one host is zero by construction; the last one or two digits may
still differ under a different compiler or linear-algebra library. Timings are
deliberately not quoted here: the benchmark protocol for those is
@sec-benchmark-protocol.

Integrated charge, split by scattering order:

| OM | position, m | $r$, m | $Q_d$, p.e. | order 0 | order 1 | order $\ge2$ | active |
|--:|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| 1 | $(25,0,-20)$ | 32.02 | $4.134\times10^{-4}$ | 0 | $6.59\times10^{-5}$ | $3.47\times10^{-4}$ | no |
| 2 | $(25,0,0)$ | 25.00 | $7.200\times10^{-3}$ | 0 | $3.169\times10^{-3}$ | $4.031\times10^{-3}$ | no |
| 3 | $(25,0,20)$ | 32.02 | $9.324\times10^{-1}$ | $5.205\times10^{-1}$ | $2.870\times10^{-1}$ | $1.249\times10^{-1}$ | yes |
| 4 | $(60,0,0)$ | 60.00 | $1.264\times10^{-3}$ | 0 | $1.498\times10^{-4}$ | $1.114\times10^{-3}$ | no |
| 5 | $(0,0,400)$ | 400.00 | --- | --- | --- | --- | no |

Three features of this table are the point of the example.

The unscattered term is zero for every module except one. Modules 1, 2 and 4 do
not lie on the Cherenkov cone of this track, so no straight line carries light
from the track to them; everything they see has been scattered at least once,
and for modules 1 and 4 the multiply-scattered part dominates the
once-scattered part. Module 3 lies on the cone and sees $0.52$ photoelectrons
of direct light, which is $56\%$ of its charge. A calculation that treated
scattered light as a correction would be wrong by orders of magnitude for three
of the four modules that see anything.

Module 5 is not computed at all. It lies 400 m away, outside the validated
radial range of the cache, and the code does not extrapolate the radial splines
silently. Instead it forms a deliberately pessimistic estimate of what the
module could possibly see --- the entire light of the event emitted
isotropically from the nearest point of the source, attenuated by absorption
alone at the smallest absorption coefficient in the band, accepted at the peak
of the angular response and at the peak of the spectral efficiency, and then
multiplied by ten --- finds it below the threshold, and records
`omitted_outside_range = 1` in the response metadata. Had the estimate been
above the threshold the run would have stopped with an error rather than
returning a number.

This is a guard with a wide margin and not a proved upper bound. It ignores
scattering both as a loss and as a delivery mechanism, and the factor of ten is
a safety margin rather than a theorem. What it buys is that the decision to
skip a module is explicit, reported and refusable, instead of a silent
extrapolation of a spline beyond the range on which it was built.

Modules 1, 2 and 4 are computed but marked inactive. Their charge is below the
$0.01$ photoelectron threshold, so their charge is kept and their time bins are
left at zero; the metadata reports `active_modules = 1` and
`threshold_pe = 0.01`. The charge column is therefore complete for the four
in-range modules while their time-bin content is not; it makes no completeness
claim for the omitted out-of-range module. @sec-weak-module-threshold states
exactly what that guarantee is and is not.

For the one active module the time distribution peaks in the bin
$[0,20)\,\mathrm{ns}$ after the first possible arrival, with $0.7868$
photoelectrons in it.

## Checks {#sec-overview-checks}

**Reproducibility.** The transport was run twice in the same process and
compared field by field; the two summaries are identical, which is what the
`--repeats` argument of the script asserts. The route contains no random
numbers, so a difference would mean a genuine defect and not noise.

**Band limit of the acceptance.** The measured Legendre coefficients of
$A(x)$ are $\alpha_0=5.52920$, $\alpha_1=2.01062$, $\alpha_2=0.20106$, with a
residual of $3.7\times10^{-13}$ above degree 2 --- consistent with the exact
values $2\pi\cdot0.88$, $2\pi\cdot0.32$ and $2\pi\cdot0.032$ obtained by hand
from a quadratic. The bandwidth is measured by the code and reported as
`detector_acceptance_degree = 2`, not assumed (@sec-directional-om).

**Charge against the time window.** For module 3 the bins sum to $0.9447$
photoelectrons against an integrated charge @eq-overview-charge of $0.9324$,
evaluated independently at $\omega=0$; the finite window therefore holds
$101.3\%$ of the charge. The excess is not a leak in the other direction:
19 of the 40 bins are negative, with a total negative mass of $0.1230$
photoelectrons, or $13\%$ of the charge. This is the ringing of a finite
frequency grid, it is neither clipped nor renormalised, and it is a real defect
of the present time-bin settings rather than a rounding artefact.
@sec-time-and-bins explains where it comes from and @sec-validation treats the
frequency grid as one line of the error budget. An integrated charge is
therefore the reliable output of this configuration and a bin-by-bin shape is
not, at this frequency resolution.

**Spectral bookkeeping.** No source element was dropped at the Cherenkov
threshold in this band (`source_elements_dropped_at_spectral_threshold = 0`,
`source_coefficient_fraction_dropped = 0`). That is a statement about
bookkeeping, not about accuracy. It says that no element of this source had to
be discarded because $\beta n_{\rm ph}\le1$ somewhere inside the band, so
nothing was thrown away unrecorded. It does **not** say that two spectral
fields represent this source exactly: they reproduce the amplitude of the
Frank--Tamm spectrum exactly, but the emission angle is held at a single
reference phase index --- `reference_phase_index = 1.35` in this run's metadata
--- so the dispersion of the Cherenkov angle across 400--550 nm is not
represented at all. The size of that omission is not measured in this chapter.
@sec-cherenkov-source states what the two-field model does and does not carry,
and @sec-validation is where its contribution to the error budget belongs.

This chapter's numbers are compared against the package's own route only. An
independent check of the multiply-scattered order against a different method is
the business of @sec-reference-solutions, and no claim of external validation
is made here.

## Range of validity {#sec-overview-validity}

The medium must be homogeneous and unbounded. Nothing in this book applies near
a boundary, in layered water, or where the detector structure shadows a module.

An exactly computed module must lie inside the radial range of the built cache,
with a margin equal to the spatial extent of the source. The run never
extrapolates a radial spline. An out-of-range module is either rejected because
its screening estimate exceeds the threshold, or omitted and reported because
the estimate lies below it, as module 5 shows. Extending the exact range means
rebuilding and re-validating the table.

The module acceptance must be band-limited, or its truncation must be chosen
deliberately. A polynomial acceptance terminates at a finite Legendre degree. A
response that is clipped to zero inside the interval does not terminate,
because clipping puts a kink in the function and the coefficients of a function
with a discontinuous derivative fall off algebraically rather than stopping.
The code measures the decay instead of assuming it and refuses to choose the
truncation itself: it asks for one explicitly and reports the residual that the
chosen truncation leaves.

The source must lie above the Cherenkov threshold throughout the chosen band,
or the elements that cross the threshold inside it must be a negligible
fraction of the light; they cannot be represented by the two spectral fields of
@sec-cherenkov-source, and the fraction that was dropped is reported.

Finally, the observable is an expectation. It carries no fluctuation, so
anything that depends on the variance of the photoelectron count --- a trigger
efficiency, a likelihood built on single-photon statistics --- needs a
distribution that this package does not provide, only its mean.

## Exercises {#sec-overview-exercises}

1. Verify the unit cancellation in @eq-overview-pe symbol by symbol, starting
   from @eq-overview-intensity, and state what changes if the intensity is
   defined without the factor $v_g$.
2. Compute $\alpha_0$, $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ by hand for
   $A(x)=0.40+0.48x+0.12x^2$, confirm them against @sec-overview-checks, and
   show that every higher coefficient vanishes identically. Then replace $A$ by
   $\max(0,\,0.36+0.52x+0.12x^2)$, which is clipped just inside $x=-1$, and
   show numerically that its coefficients no longer terminate. Estimate the
   power of the degree at which they fall off, and relate it to the order of
   the derivative that the clipping makes discontinuous.
3. Rerun the worked example with the far module moved from 400 m to 150 m and
   predict, before running, whether it will be computed, and whether it will be
   active.
4. Halve the frequency step by doubling the number of frequencies at fixed
   maximum, rerun, and report how the negative bin mass of module 3 changes.
   State whether the integrated charge changes as well, and explain why it
   should or should not.
5. For module 1, estimate the ratio of the once-scattered to the
   multiply-scattered charge from the scattering length alone, and compare with
   the table. Explain the direction of the discrepancy.

This chapter's companion is the script named in @sec-overview-example rather
than a notebook; the notebook sequence begins with @sec-spectral-rte.
